title: What a fraction measures
objectives: Read a fraction as a number of equal parts of one whole
Place a fraction on a number line, including one above 1
Find a fraction of an amount of money

screens.title: What a fraction measures
screens.prose: Cut one whole into equal pieces and count some of them. That is all a fraction is. We will see why both the count and the piece size matter.
Two identical chocolate bars. Bar A snaps into 4 equal pieces. Bar B snaps into 8 equal pieces. The picture shows bar B.

state.caption: Your friend eats the 3 shaded pieces of bar B

screens.question: You eat 3 pieces of bar A. Who eats more chocolate?

options.why: You compared the counts, 3 and 3. A piece of bar A is twice the size of a piece of bar B.
You read 8 as more chocolate than 4. Cutting the same bar into more pieces makes each piece smaller.

hints.text: Which bar has the bigger pieces?
Two pieces of bar B make one piece of bar A.
Your 3 pieces of bar A match 6 pieces of bar B. Compare 6 with 3.

feedback.correct: Your pieces are twice the size, so 3 of them is more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the size of a piece of each bar, not just the counts.

explain.text: You compared piece sizes, not just counts. The hatched strip lays your 3 pieces of bar A over bar B: they cover 6 of its 8 pieces. A count of pieces means nothing until you know how big each piece is.

canvas.caption: Hatched: your 3 pieces of bar A

screens.prose: This bar snaps into 6 equal pieces. You eat it from the left end, one piece at a time. Tap a piece to shade it, and tap again to clear it.
screens.question: Shade the pieces you eat if you eat exactly half the bar.

hints.text: Half means two equal parts. How many pieces would each part get?
Half the bar ends after this piece.
Six pieces in two equal parts is 3 pieces each. Shade the first 3.

feedback.correct: Three pieces eaten, three left: two equal parts.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade from the left until the shaded part and the rest are the same size.

byKey.two: You shaded 2 pieces, perhaps for the 2 in one half. Half of 6 pieces is 3 pieces.
byKey.one: You shaded 1 piece, perhaps for the 1 in one half. Half of 6 pieces is 3 pieces.
byKey.c14: You shaded a piece past the middle. Eating from the left, half the bar ends after piece 3.
byKey.c15: You shaded a piece past the middle. Eating from the left, half the bar ends after piece 3.
byKey.c16: You shaded a piece past the middle. Eating from the left, half the bar ends after piece 3.

explain.text: You shaded 3 of the 6 pieces, and 3 are left. The two parts are equal, so this is half the bar. Each piece is one sixth of the bar, and you have three of them.

screens.prose: We write the half you shaded as $\tfrac{3}{6}$, said "three sixths". The bottom number says how many equal pieces make one whole. The top number counts the pieces you have. This is a **fraction**.
screens.question: What fraction of this bar is shaded?

hints.text: How many equal pieces make the whole bar?
These are the shaded pieces.
The bar has 5 pieces and 2 are shaded. Write 2 over 5 as 2/5.

feedback.correct: Two of the five equal pieces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the shaded pieces on top and every piece of the bar on the bottom.

byKey.vs-rest: You put the 3 unshaded pieces on the bottom. The bottom counts every piece in the whole bar.
byKey.rest: You counted the unshaded pieces on top. The top counts the shaded ones.
byKey.flipped: You put the 5 on top. The whole bar goes on the bottom, and the shaded pieces on top.

explain.text: You counted 5 equal pieces in the whole and 2 shaded. So the shaded part is $\tfrac{2}{5}$, two fifths. Each piece is $\tfrac{1}{5}$ of the bar, and you have two of them.

screens.prose: A fraction is also a distance along a line. Here the stretch from 0 to 1 is one whole, like the bar. It is cut into 5 equal steps.
screens.question: Drag the point to $\tfrac{2}{5}$.

hints.text: How many steps make the whole from 0 to 1?
Start at 0. Each gap between two marks is one fifth.
Two steps from 0 is two fifths. Count gaps, not marks.

feedback.correct: Two steps of one fifth from 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count 2 equal steps along from 0.

byKey.ticks: You counted 2 marks, starting with the mark at 0. Count steps, the gaps between marks.
byKey.from-one: You counted 2 steps back from 1. Fractions are measured from 0.

explain.text: You moved 2 steps of one fifth each from 0. The point sits where a bar of $\tfrac{2}{5}$ would end. On a line, a fraction is how far you are from 0.

screens.prose: This line is cut into 8 equal steps. A fraction does not have to use the same steps as the marks on the line.
screens.question: Drag the point to $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

hints.text: How many of these small steps make one quarter?
Half way to 1 is two quarters.
Each quarter is 2 small steps. Three quarters is 6 small steps from 0.

feedback.correct: Three quarters is 6 of the 8 small steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cut the whole into 4 equal parts first, then take 3.

byKey.eighths: You moved 3 of the small steps. Those are eighths, because 8 make the whole. A quarter is 2 of them.
byKey.four: You moved 4 small steps, perhaps for the 4 in three quarters. That is half the whole, two quarters.

explain.text: Each quarter covers 2 small steps, so $\tfrac{3}{4}$ sits 6 steps from 0. The marks on a line need not match the fraction. Cut the whole into the fraction's own equal parts.

screens.prose: A fraction can pass 1. This line runs from 0 to 2, and each whole is cut into 4 equal steps.
screens.question: Drag the point to $\tfrac{5}{4}$.

hints.text: How many quarters make one whole?
One whole is 4 quarters. It ends at the mark labelled 1.
Count 5 quarter steps from 0. You pass 1 after 4 of them.

feedback.correct: Four quarters reach 1, and one more quarter passes it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count 5 quarter steps from 0.

byKey.stop-one: You stopped at 1, which is 4 quarters. Five quarters is one more quarter past it.
byKey.one-quarter: You went 1 step, as if the fraction were one quarter. Five quarters is 5 steps.

explain.text: Four quarters fill one whole, so $\tfrac{5}{4}$ is one whole and one quarter more. When the top is bigger than the bottom, the amount is more than one whole. A fraction is not always a part of one thing.

screens.prose: This bar was snapped into 3 pieces, and one piece is shaded. Someone says the shaded part is $\tfrac{1}{3}$ of the bar.
screens.question: How much of the bar is shaded?

options.why: You counted 1 piece out of 3. That works only when the pieces are equal, and these are not.
You used the size of a small piece. The shaded piece is as big as two small pieces.

hints.text: Are the three pieces the same size?
The shaded piece is as long as these two pieces together.
The shaded piece matches the other two together. So it is one of two equal halves.

feedback.correct: The shaded piece is as big as the rest of the bar.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the shaded piece with the rest of the bar.

byKey.third: You counted 1 piece of 3 and called it a third. The pieces are not equal, so the count does not give the amount.

explain.text: You compared the shaded piece with the rest, not the count. It equals the other two pieces together, so it is half. A fraction needs equal pieces, so unequal pieces must be cut equal first.

canvas.caption: Cut into 4 equal pieces: the shaded part is 2 of them

screens.prose: Every time, you did two things. You cut one whole into equal pieces, then counted the pieces you have. $$\text{fraction} = \frac{\text{pieces you have}}{\text{equal pieces in one whole}}$$ The bottom sets the size of each piece. The top counts them.
screens.question: In $\tfrac{7}{10}$, what does the 10 tell you?

options.text: The whole is cut into 10 equal pieces

options.why: You read the bottom as the pieces you have. The top, 7, counts those.
You read the bottom as what is left. It counts every piece in the whole, so 3 are left.

hints.text: On the bar with 2 of 5 pieces shaded, where did the 5 go?
The bottom always counted every equal piece in the whole bar.

feedback.correct: The bottom number sets the size of each piece.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what you put on the bottom for the bar with 5 pieces.

explain.text: In $\tfrac{2}{5}$ you put the 5 equal pieces of the whole on the bottom. So the 10 in $\tfrac{7}{10}$ cuts the whole into tenths, and the 7 counts them. Seven tenths leaves 3 tenths over.

screens.prose: A small trading fund made £12 profit this week. The profit is split into 4 equal shares, and you own 3 of the shares.
screens.question: How much of the profit is yours, in pounds?

hints.text: How much is one share worth?
The whole bar is the £12, cut into 4 equal shares.
One share is £12 split 4 ways, which is £3. You own 3 shares.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what one share is worth, then count your shares.

byKey.shares: You gave the number of shares you own. Each share is worth some pounds: £12 split 4 ways.
byKey.by-three: You split £12 into 3 parts. The profit is split into 4 shares, and you own 3 of them.
byKey.times: You multiplied £12 by 3. That is three whole profits; you own part of one.

explain.text: You split £12 into 4 equal shares of £3 and took 3 of them. So $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of £12 is £9. A fraction of an amount is a count of equal shares of it.

ideas: A fraction counts equal pieces of one whole. The bottom says how many pieces make the whole; the top counts the ones you have.
On a number line, a fraction is a distance from 0, measured in the fraction's own equal steps.
When the top is bigger than the bottom, the amount is more than one whole.

formula.name: Reading a fraction
formula.tex: \frac{\text{pieces you have}}{\text{equal pieces in one whole}}
formula.note: The pieces must be equal. $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of £12 is 3 shares of £3.

summary.trap: Counting pieces gives a fraction only when the pieces are equal. One of three unequal pieces need not be a third.

quiz.prose: This rectangle is cut into equal pieces.
quiz.question: What fraction of the rectangle is shaded?

options.why: You put the 5 unshaded pieces on the bottom. The bottom counts all 8 pieces.
You took one row of 4 as the whole. The whole has 2 rows of 4.
You counted the unshaded pieces on top. The top counts the shaded ones.

feedback.correct: Three of the eight equal pieces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every piece for the bottom and the shaded ones for the top.

explain.text: The rectangle has 2 rows of 4, so 8 equal pieces. Three are shaded, so the fraction is $\tfrac{3}{8}$.

quiz.prose: The line from 0 to 1 is cut into equal steps.
quiz.question: Which fraction is at the point?

options.why: You counted the 4 marks, not the 3 equal steps between them.
You put the steps on top. The whole is cut into 3 steps, so 3 goes on the bottom.

feedback.correct: Two of the three equal steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the steps from 0 to 1, then the steps from 0 to the point.

explain.text: Three equal steps make the whole, so each is a third. The point is 2 steps from 0, at $\tfrac{2}{3}$.

quiz.prose: Two identical pizzas. One is cut into 3 equal slices, the other into 5 equal slices.
quiz.question: Which slice is bigger?

options.text: A slice of the pizza cut into 3, $\tfrac{1}{3}$
A slice of the pizza cut into 5, $\tfrac{1}{5}$
options.why: You read 5 as more than 3. More slices from the same pizza means smaller slices.
You saw one slice each. The pizzas are cut into different numbers of slices, so the slices differ.

feedback.correct: Fewer slices from the same pizza means bigger slices.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what happens to each slice as you cut more of them.

explain.text: The same pizza shared 3 ways gives bigger slices than shared 5 ways. So $\tfrac{1}{3}$ is more than $\tfrac{1}{5}$, even though 3 is less than 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one fifth of £20 first.

byKey.one-part: That is one fifth, one part. Two fifths is two parts.
byKey.half: You took half of £20. Two fifths is a little less than a half.
byKey.times: You doubled £20. Two fifths is a part of £20, so it is less than £20.

explain.text: One fifth of £20 is £4, because 5 parts of £4 make £20. Two fifths is 2 of those parts: £8.

quiz.question: Which of these amounts is more than one whole?

options.why: You saw a 7. Here only 4 of 7 equal pieces are taken, which is less than one whole.
Three thirds is all three pieces: exactly one whole, not more.

feedback.correct: Seven quarters is one whole and three quarters more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the top with the bottom.

explain.text: Four quarters make one whole, so $\tfrac{7}{4}$ is more than one. When the top is bigger than the bottom, the amount passes one whole.
